verdict: Built the regulatory-sign annotation — the missing piece for GAIN-of-function — from UniProt 'Activity regulation' text, which encodes each protein's breakable BRAKE (autoinhibition / intramolecular repression / inactive conformation). Tested against real GOF/LOF ground truth (UniProt PROTO-ONCOGENE vs TUMOR-SUPPRESSOR keywords). RESULT, read the fair way (a rare, high-confidence flag): when the regulatory sign FIRES — i.e. we can annotate a breakable brake — the gene is GOF with PRECISION 86% (19 oncogenes vs 3 tumour suppressors flagged), a 5.4x enrichment; and the examples are textbook autoinhibited oncogenes (ABL1 'stabilized in the inactive form', KIT/PDGFRA/FGFR2 'inactive conformation in the absence of ligand', BRAF 'maintained in an inactive state via an intramolecular interaction'). So the sign is a HIGH-PRECISION directional GOF caller: where a breakable brake is annotated, disrupting it flips a structural BREAK into a functional GAIN — exactly the capability scale alone could never add (a break is a break; only the sign says up vs down). Its limit is RECALL: only 10% of GOF genes have the brake annotated in this one source (which is why the AUC is just 0.54 — dragged down by the un-annotated 0s, not by wrong calls). So it is annotation-limited, not mechanism-limited — an information gap, not a compute gap, exactly as predicted. Wired into NEXUS: a mutation disrupting a brake-bearing (inhibitory) interface pushes activity UP (GOF) instead of down; where no sign is annotated it defaults to LOF-only. Raising recall means broadening the sign sources (autoinhibitory structural annotations, signed signalling DBs like SIGNOR) — more information, not more compute. HONEST LIMITS: this is the PROTEIN-level sign (has a brake), not the per-INTERFACE sign (which specific interface is the brake) — that finer resolution needs structural annotation of the autoinhibitory contact; and the oncogene/TSG label is a gene-level GOF/LOF proxy, not a per-mutation one.
